newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jewish settlers hope to keep peace moves on ice.
newsitem.headline: Jewish settlers hope to keep peace moves on ice.

text.p: Jewish settlers and their allies in Israel's government say their threat to oust Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from office has succeeded in freezing a peace process they view as seriously flawed.
They hope their strategy will soon bury it once and for all.
They say the 47-year-old prime minister they worked hard to elect last May is a puzzle who bears watching and that they may have to fight him again if he veers off the right-wing path.

For now they have stopped a drive to oust Netanyahu, a campaign they say forced him to approve building a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem which Arabs call Jabal Abu Ghneim and Israelis call Har Homa.
But they vow to renew the fight if he bends to U.S. pressure to make conciliatory gestures to the Palestinians.
"You see, I haven't to wait long. Mr Ross is on his way," settler strategist Eliakim Haetzni told Reuters.

U.S. envoy Dennis Ross's trip was spurred by clashes between Palestinians and Israeli troops over the settlement that entered an eighth day on Thursday, and an Islamist bombing last Friday that killed three Israelis.

Settler advocates, who believe the West Bank and Gaza Strip where Palestinians want to establish a state are the Jewish people's by biblical birthright, could barely contain their satisfaction this week over crumbling peace moves.
More than 130,000 Jews have settled amid some two million Palestinians in the areas since Israel captured them in 1967.

"There is a difference of night and day. The prime minister is acting as we expected him to," said lawmaker Shaul Yahalom, of the National Religious Party (NRP), a key coalition member. Before Har Homa, Yahalom had pushed for Netanyahu to be ousted.
He said now that talks with the Palestinians based on a 1993 accord had broken down over Har Homa, they must never resume.
Michael Kleiner, of Netanyahu's own Likud-Gesher-Tsomet alignment, agreed.
"We think Oslo is dead," said Kleiner, who heads a group that threatened to vote against Netanyahu in parliament if he did not build Har Homa.

Israel and the PLO hammered out the 1993 peace deal in Oslo. Netanyahu campaigned for election last May saying the deal was a disaster and narrowly edged out Labour Prime Minister Shimon Peres, an architect of the Oslo accords.

Settler advocates say an interim accord calling for three further Israeli West Bank pullbacks must be dropped. Netanyahu sealed that accord in January. But this month, after building began at Har Homa, Netanyahu suggested dropping the interim deal to move to accelerated talks on a final peace accord.

If peace talks resume, settler advocates say, they must be final negotiations aimed at leaving the Palestinian Authority, which already controls eight West Bank cities and much of the Gaza Strip, with nothing more than it already has.
Haetzni said the interim deal only fed the Palestinian "tiger" which he said had one goal -- Israel's destruction.
"In Jerusalem now, at Har Homa, Netanyahu stopped feeding the tiger," he said. Asked what would be the next step, he said: "Put the tiger into a cage, and God forbid, not a large cage."
Local media say Netanyahu might form a "national unity" government with the Labour Party to lift right-wing pressure.
Haetzni said: "It is very difficult to fathom this man...No one knows who he's fooling: the ministers he met today whom he told this (about national unity) is baloney -- or Mr Peres.
"Or does he fool himself?" asked Haetzni.
The lesson learned from Har Homa about Netanyahu was that "if something motivates him, it is naked power," Haetzni said.

If Netanyahu bowed to U.S. pressure to placate Palestinians or tried to form a unity government, the NRP and Likud rebels would work to bring him down, making clear to him, Haetzni said, that "You can go to outer space but you have no place to return."
